national.title: NPR's Senior Podcast Challenge: Early entries we love
national.summary: People 65 and older have been submitting stories for a chance to win our grand prize — a visit to NPR watch your podcast air live on Weekend Edition . There's still time to enter!
national.body:
Tatyana Alanis/NPR Once people hit retirement age, there are so many questions: Who am I without my job? What do I do to fill this time? How are my relationships changing?

This fall, for the first-ever NPR Senior Podcast Challenge , we asked those of you in the over-65 crowd, to tell us about all this, and you've been sending in your answers.

The competition flips the story line on our popular NPR Student Podcast Challenge – since 2018 more than 90,000 young people have sent us their stories , in their own voices .

Only on NPR 65 or older, with a story to tell? Submit your podcast for a chance to hear it on NPR Now, we're hearing from listeners with a lot of experience, hopefully some wisdom, and perhaps more grey hair.

While the contest is still open for a few more weeks — you have until November 30 to enter — we've been listening to more than 100 podcasts that have come in so far.

Lou Ann Baylock, of Sarasota, Fla., told us she wasn't too happy about the title of our contest: the "senior" part.

"I'm 68, but I'm NOT a senior, am I?" she asks in her podcast, Talk to Me .

"I thought seniors were people in their 80s," she says. "I mean, I see my body changing. I know I'm getting older. But am I really a senior?"

national.title: South Korea education minister resigns over exam cheating scandal
national.summary: Choi Kyo-jin admits last-minute measures to stop AI-assisted cheating during the college entrance exam caused chaos.
national.body:
South Korea's Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin has resigned over an exam cheating scandal that shocked the nation.

He said he took full responsibility for the confusion caused by last-minute measures aimed at stopping AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's annual college entrance exam, known as Suneung.

A week ago, the top scorer in the national tax accountancy exam admitted using a mini-camera, mobile phone and AI tools. This prompted officials to act urgently to detect hidden devices, including sending emergency alerts to every single mobile phone in the country.

The Suneung takes up to nine hours to complete, and it plays a big role in career trajectories of millions of South Koreans.

"As the minister in charge, I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance," Choi was quoted as saying on Sunday by South Korea's Yonhap's news agency.

"Now that the exam has concluded, I feel a deep sense of responsibility and am offering my resignation," the minister added.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung - who has been calling for an overhaul of the current exam system - later accepted Choi's resignation.

The education ministry earlier said 111 candidates had been found with unauthorised smart devices during this year's Suneung, which was taken by about 500,000 students.

national.title: Italian jeweller and businessman Paolo Bulgari dies aged 89
national.summary: In a statement to Italian media, his family remember him as "the greatest jeweller of our time".
national.body:
Italian jeweller Paolo Bulgari, who helped turn his family's business into a global luxury brand, has died in Rome aged age 89.

His family announced the news, remembering him as "the greatest jeweller of our time", according to Italian media.

Paolo Bulgari was Chairman of the Bvlgari Group since 1984 and its jewellery pieces have adorned Hollywood stars and royalty including Diana, Princess of Wales.

The company Bvlgari posted an online tribute to the "true creative soul", whose work would "continue to inspire generations to come".

The firm, Bulgari, was set up by his grandfather, Greek silversmith Sotirios Voulgaris, in Rome in the late 19th century - who later adapted his name to Bulgari in Italian.

Originally from Paramythia, a mountain village in the Epirus region of northwestern Greece renowned for its silver jewellery, Voulgaris fled Ottoman rule and settled in Naples before opening a shop in Rome.

Paolo Bulgari joined the company shortly after leaving school, becoming an expert in gemstones - eventually leading the business and overseeing international growth.

The Bulgari family favoured bold gemstones, rich yellow gold, generous proportions and unexpected colour combinations to set them apart from the delicate asethetic associated with Parisian jewellery houses.

national.title: Three killed and dozens missing after fire at Indonesian factory
national.summary: At least three people were killed and 36 are still missing after a fire at a confectionary factory.
national.body:
At least three people have been killed and 36 are still missing after a fire at a confectionary factory in western Java on Saturday.

Firefighters were still tackling some flames on Sunday, while rescuers searched for the missing in parts of the damaged building where workers were believed to be trapped.

Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency said on Sunday 15 survivors had been located, and four others taken to hospital and a local clinic with undisclosed injuries.

The factory is in Serang district, Banten province, about 50km (31km) west of Jakarta. Authorities have not yet determined the fire's cause.

Banten Governor, Andra Soni, told media about 60 people were believed to be inside the factory when it caught fire on Saturday evening.

"All members of the joint SAR team are making every effort to locate the missing victims while prioritising the safety of personnel on the ground," the rescue agency said.

Relatives of the missing workers had gathered outside the factory waiting for updates, according to local broadcasts cited by AFP.

Firefighters had been called to the building at 16:30 local time (09:30 GMT) on Saturday - but it was already engulfed in flames, broadcaster Kompas TV reported, citing fire official Tubugas Machfudz.

national.summary: The Kansas City Current made history Saturday, capturing their first NWSL Championship title with a 2-1 win over the Washington Spirit.

Kansas City's Debinha scored in the 97th minute of stoppage time to extend the lead. The Spirit's star forward Trinity Rodman pulled one back in the 98th minute, but it was too little too late. The first half was physical, with fouls traded back and forth. Despite having less possession, Kansas City posed the greater offensive threat. The Spirit, meanwhile, struggled to capitalize on their time with the ball and recorded no shots on target in the first 45 minutes of the match.Rodman took a hard hit from behind by Kansas City's Laney Rouse just five minutes into the match. Although she was able to continue playing, Rodman appeared bothered by her left arm and spent much of the first half stretching it before returning to play.The Current, who were founded as an expansion franchise in 2021, were playing in their second ever championship game. They fell to the Orlando Pride in 2024, and Gotham FC in 2025. national.title: Mexican drug lord on FBI's 10 most wanted list arrested in shoot-out
national.summary: Fausto Isidro "Chapo Idisro" Meza Flores, who is accused of drug trafficking and torture, is detained after gun fight with authorities.
national.body:
A Mexican drug lord who was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list has been arrested following a shoot-out with Mexican authorities.

Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores and seven others were detained by Mexican special forces in Guasave, Sinaloa on Friday, Mexico's defence secretariat said.

Seven suspects were killed in the operation, as were four members of the Mexican army who were travelling to reinforce security in Guasave, the secretariat added.

Meza Flores was wanted in Mexico on organised crime charges, while he has been accused of "flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and other deadly drugs" by the FBI. The US is seeking his extradition.

Mexico has stepped up efforts to tackle drug-related crime after coming under pressure from US President Donald Trump since he returned to the White House.

Meza Flores, the leader of the Meza Flores Organisation, also known as the Guasave Cartel, is thought to have been active in the drug trafficking trade since the 1990s but managed to evade authorities till now by maintaining a relatively low profile.

Using US intelligence on his whereabouts, Mexican special forces descended on his location using "stealth and surprise", establishing a perimeter to prevent him from escaping and reinforcements arriving, Mexico's defence secretariat said.

However, they "came under attack from gunfire and explosives" before entering the property and arresting Meza Flores, the secretariat continued.

national.title: FBI reportedly investigating apparent hack of its criminal database
national.summary: The National Crime Information Center database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information.
national.body:
The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its criminal information database, US media reports, citing two people briefed on the issue.

The National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information on warrants and background checks.

It would not be the first time hackers have targeted the FBI, the domestic intelligence and security service of the US. The agency did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

When asked about the breach in a Fox News interview on Saturday, President Donald Trump said he had "just heard" about the hack. "I will say that it's not good. I don't like that," he said.

"But maybe we'll learn things that we would've never learned otherwise," Trump added.

This apparent breach of FBI database comes after a string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors in the US last week. Officials have said they were not caused by cyber-attacks, but the blackouts have sparked scrutiny from lawmakers.

White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired this week, with Trump saying he was not good enough.

Dan Lorhmann, a former analyst for the National Security Agency (NSA), told the BBC News Channel that the NCIC's data included "critical information relating to nationwide criminal activity" and needed to be protected.

national.title: Nigerian youth have shown their power in the past - why aren't they shaping this election?
national.summary: Fewer young people have registered to vote in next year's election than in 2023 - are young people losing faith in democracy?
national.body:
Abdulhadi Dalhatu is something of a rarity in Nigeria politics.

At 38, he is among the young people seeking elected office in a country where about 80% of the population is under 40.

He hopes his age will stand in his favour as he campaigns for a seat in the state assembly in the northern Kano state in January's general elections.

"Younger people are the majority in this country and should be deciding the future," Dalhatu tells the BBC.

But Nigeria's political history suggests he faces an uphill battle.

Since the return to civilian rule in 1999, Goodluck Jonathan has been the youngest person elected president, taking office at the age of 53.

The current president, Bola Tinubu, is 74 and would be 79 by the end of a second term if he is re-elected in January.

His main challengers are also considerably older. Atiku Abubakar, seeking the presidency for the seventh time, is 79, while Peter Obi is 65.

national.title: How a teen gamer and his mother helped rescue a missing girl
national.summary: When 16-year-old Landon Tresp met a teenage girl in an online game, it led to him and his mother helping the FBI rescue her from kidnapping.
national.body:
Sixteen-year-old Landon Tresp was in the bedroom of his family's Colorado mountain home, playing an online game after finishing his daily chores, when he began chatting on his laptop with another player.

She was also a teenager, and the pair "kind of just clicked," he tells the BBC.

He told her he liked her name, and she confessed that it was an alias. She was a runaway, she said - and was being held against her will, hundreds of miles from home, though she didn't know exactly where. The girl, 17, and had been missing for more than a year.

Stunned, Landon felt "helpless," he says - and, after learning more details over two weeks of chatting, he decided to tell his mother, Khristina on 31 October this year. The 41-year-old nurse and mother of five was putting Halloween makeup on her younger children for trick-or-treating when he briefed her.

That set the mother and son on a path to track down his friend, contact her mother, cooperate with the FBI - and ultimately witness the rescue of the teen - only 24 hours after Landon first alerted Khristina to her plight.

"She had one opportunity to reach out her hand and ask for help, and she chose me," Khristina says of the girl, who was 15 when she went missing.

The Tresps have shared with BBC screenshots of communication with the girl and a photo matching the criminal complaint to corroborate their story.

Landon first told his mother about "Jenny" - whose identity the BBC is protecting - in mid-October, a few weeks before the rescue.

national.title: Princeton student detained by ICE at Reagan Airport after conference
national.summary: Eva Yi Xie, a third-year Ph.D. Princeton student, was detained following a presentation she gave at the Society for Neuroscience.
national.body: A Princeton University student was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement this week at Ronald Reagan National Airport in Washington, D.C., after attending a neuroscience conference, the school and her colleagues said.Eva Yi Xie, a third-year Ph.D. student, was detained on Thursday night following a presentation she gave at the Society for Neuroscience, her colleague wrote on X. "News of Eva's detention is distressing for me and many members of the Princeton University community," Rodney Priestley, the dean of the Princeton graduate school, said in a statement. "The University has arranged for Eva to be represented by legal counsel, and we will remain in contact with her legal team, her family, and colleagues to provide support. We hope Eva will soon be able to resume her studies at Princeton." A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said in a statement that Xie was taken into custody during a "targeted immigration enforcement operation" at Reagan Airport. Xie was admitted to the United States on a temporary basis on March 16, 2016, according to DHS, which said she is a Chinese national. DHS said Xie had been required to depart the U.S. by Sept. 15, 2016. "Xie will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending her removal proceedings," DHS said in a statement. "Xie has NEVER held valid authorization to study in the United States. To be clear, a pending application does not confer legal status in the United States."Carlos Brody, of the Princeton Neuroscience Institute, wrote on X that Xie sent her lab mates a Slack message for help before she was detained. She's being held in Chantilly, Virginia, according to Brody. "Her lawyers are working on her release," Brody wrote. "She's a brilliant neuroscientist, mentor, and friend. She went to a conference to present her work, and now she's in a detention center. She should be home."Xie's attorney, Kerry Doyle, said in a statement that her "arrest and detention is without legal basis.""They cannot arrest people without a warrant if they are not a flight risk or danger to the community," Doyle said. "She is neither. She's a star rising scientist with permission to be in the US and they grabbed her because she is easy pickings at an airport where TSA and ICE are sharing information and targeting unsuspecting travelers with authorization to be in the US."

national.title: Why do people believe recent tech failures must be connected?
national.summary: Even without clear evidence, people drew connections between recent tech failures and outages. The way our brains and social media platforms work helps explain why.
national.body:
Companies including Microsoft, United Airlines, JPMorgan Chase and U.S. Bank experienced technical issues and outages that caused widespread banking issues, delayed plane departures and interrupted workdays across the world. Soon after, Marriott and Apple customers also experienced digital problems, and 178 companies reported being affected by a Nov. 16 cyberattack.

At the same time, various U.S. government systems — the Federal Aviation Administration, National Security Agency and National Weather Service — fell into disarray, including a rare nationwide ground stop. For many people, the pile-on of concerning news alerts had a sinister feel.

WATCH: Mounting tech disruptions raise concerns about U.S. cybersecurity

"We're under attack in a way we've never seen before," wrote Nalin Haley, a conservative influencer and son of Republican politician Nikki Haley, on Nov. 17. "This is an AI cyberattack."

On Bluesky, Christopher Webb, a self-described "lifelong Dem" and party strategist, questioned whether the issues were connected.

"Coincidence??? 4 major banks reporting outages, a massive Microsoft disruption, and a nationwide FAA ground stop, all within days of each other," he wrote Nov. 16.

The best available information points to mundane explanations such as routine maintenance, one-off problems or isolated cyberattacks, rather than an imminent systemic collapse or a coordinated attack on digital systems.

The rapid-fire succession of events didn't help. Neither did the timing of a planned, routine Nov. 17 test of the country's Emergency Alert System.

national.title: For families of the fallen, Trump's proposed arch casts a shadow over Arlington National Cemetery
national.summary: Trump's proposed 250-foot-tall arch could cast a long shadow on Arlington National Cemetery, with the potential to literally shade gravesites, disrupt solemn visits with the noise of construction and alter the carefully designed historic landscape of the nation's capital.
national.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Cpl. Spencer Collart's headstone faces the rising sun and the Lincoln Memorial to the east. The Marine Corps War Memorial is nearby. Soon, President Donald Trump's gilded, towering arch could be, too.

Collart's silent stone speaks volumes in its simplicity of courage, sacrifice and loss. It stands among thousands of uniform headstones and other monuments, each telling the story of the person, or persons, beneath it.

WATCH: 2nd judge blocks construction of Trump's arch in D.C.

But if Trump gets his way, a different story may be told. His proposed 250-foot-tall (76-meter-tall) arch could cast a long shadow on Arlington National Cemetery, with the potential to literally shade gravesites, disrupt solemn visits with the noise of construction and alter the carefully designed historic landscape of the nation's capital.

For many veterans and their families, and the loved ones of others buried at the cemetery, the arch has no place so close to the Arlington, Virginia, burial grounds. That opposition has sparked lawsuits by veterans groups and others, including nine family members of the Kennedy political dynasty, who argue the arch, which would be built on a traffic circle about half a mile (0.8 kilometers) from Arlington's main entrance, will fundamentally change the experience of visiting the cemetery.

"It's a billboard for an ego. It's a loud, boastful, gaudy piece of marketing dropped onto sacred ground," said Bart Collart, Spencer's father. His son, a young Marine who died at 21 trying to save fellow crew members in a 2023 Osprey crash in Australia, would see it as "dirtying hallowed ground."

The arch project is part of a series of renovations to Washington that Trump, a Republican, has set in motion to reimagine the city. When complete, the gold and granite arch will stretch taller than the Lincoln Memorial.

Opponents say the arch would break the alignment between the Lincoln Memorial, the Memorial Bridge and Arlington House, which was formerly Confederate Gen. Robert E. Lee's home, and the symbolism of a reunited North and South.

national.title: Trump orders federal contractors to check with White House before responding to Congress
national.summary: President Trump is directing federal contractors to consult the White House about inquiries from Congress and to withhold any communications that his administration considers privileged.
national.body:
President Trump speaks at a news conference in the James Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House, Friday, Nov. 20, 2026, in Washington. Jacquelyn Martin/AP hide caption

NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump is directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold any communications that the White House considers privileged, according to a new executive order .

The companies must also coordinate with the White House and U.S. agencies on "appropriate responses" to any such requests, the order issued late Friday says. If they fail to comply, the White House warns their contracts could be terminated and their future work with the federal government suspended.

The order is the Republican administration's latest effort to resist what are expected to be wide-ranging and aggressive oversight efforts from Democrats when they take over Congress in January. Democrats have made government contracts one of their top investigative targets , noting that federal money has been flowing to companies linked with Trump's family, particularly at the Pentagon.

national.title: Lock of former US President George Washington's hair sells for $4,000
national.summary: The hair was given as a sign of friendship shortly before Washington's death in 1799, according to a descendent of its former owner.
national.body:
A framed lock of hair from America's first president, George Washington, has been sold at auction for $4,000 (£3,058).

The hair once belonged to John Gadsby, who entertained Washington in 1799 just before the latter's death the same year, and was later obtained by a collector called John K Lattimer from a descendent of Gadsby's, according to Richmond Auctions, which sold the item.

Saturday's sale is not the most expensive for Washington hair at auction. Three strands thought to have been removed from him close to or after his death stored in a locket sold for nearly $40,000 in 2021.

Gadsby, a resident of what in 1799 was the town of Alexandria in Virginia, entertained Washington for dinner shortly before his death later that year, according to a testament given in 1928 by Gadsby's granddaughter, Julia Ten Eyck McBlair, and which was posted on the Richmond Auctions website.

McBlair stated that her grandfather came into possession of Washington's hair "in view of the friendship and association with his last days" and had it framed and hung "under General Washington's portrait in our home in Washington City, there I have seen it all my life".

Gadsby hosted Washington's two birthday celebrations in 1798 and 1799, Richmond Auctions states.

Washington led American forces to victory against the British in the War of Independence and helped draft the US Constitution before becoming the country's first president in 1788. He stepped down in 1797 after serving two terms.

Several locks of Washington's hair have been preserved, including at least 50 examples that are in a collection at his former residence, Mount Vernon, which is now a museum.

national.body: Britain's Catherine, Princess of Wales, opens up about finding hope and joy amid uncertainty in a new documentary exploring life since her cancer diagnosis in 2024."Heal" follows 44-year-old Catherine as she attempts the Three Peaks Challenge, climbing the highest mountains in Scotland, England and Wales within 24 hours.The Princess of Wales said at the time she undertook the challenge in support of the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, an organization connected to the hospital where she received her treatment. She was greeted by her husband Prince William, who is heir to the throne, and their children Princes George and Louis and Princess Charlotte, as well as her parents and brother after completing the climb. In a trailer released Saturday by Prince William and Catherine's Kensington Palace office, the princess reflects on her cancer journey and speaks to others about their experiences.Catherine announced in March 2024 that she had cancer and was undergoing chemotherapy following major abdominal surgery. She did not reveal what type of cancer she was treated for.Catherine disclosed in January 2025 that she was in remission about 10 months after announcing her diagnosis. At the time, she said in her post on Instagram that she remains focused on recovery: "As anyone who has experienced a cancer diagnosis will know, it takes time to adjust to a new normal."She has gradually resumed her public duties, visiting India with William earlier this month.In the trailer, Catherine says cancer changes people profoundly, and "healing is a journey. How to reconnect with the things you once knew, and how to find a sense of hope and joy alongside uncertainty."She adds that "it's clear we're not meant to carry life's challenges alone" and "often, it is through pain that we realize there's a greater beauty that lies beyond that."The film will premiere on the BBC in the United Kingdom on Nov. 29, before airing internationally on NBCUniversal in the United States on Nov. 30.

national.title: Trump vows to work with Democrats to cap credit card interest rates at 10%
national.summary: The standard proposal would substantially reduce what credit card companies can charge customers. The median credit card interest rate is roughly 22.2%, according to an August survey by the New York Federal Reserve.
national.body:
NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump said Saturday that he would work with the incoming Democratic Congress to cap credit card interest rates, hoping to fulfill a promise he made on the 2024 campaign trail but couldn't deliver on because of industry pressure and a lack of interest from his fellow Republicans.

"I would do it. These credit card companies have made a lot," Trump told Fox News Channel's "Saturday in America."

Democrats and the Republican president have both backed capping credit card interest rates, with the standard proposal being capping rates at 10%. It would substantially reduce what credit card companies can charge customers. The median credit card interest rate is roughly 22.2%, according to an August survey by the New York Federal Reserve.

Trump proposed capping credit card interest rates in January , as part of the White House's affordability push. Banks and credit card companies immediately and aggressively opposed the proposal, saying any interest rate cap would force them to cancel cards for the poor and less creditworthy customers or substantially cut back on the rewards they offer when customers spend on their cards.

The proposal also did not sit well with Republicans, and there was little effort by the GOP-controlled Congress to fulfill Trump's promise.

That could change now that Democrats will control both the House and Senate. Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., who is expected to be the next chair of the Senate Banking Committee, has said repeatedly she wants to cap rates.

In response to the Fox News interview, Warren said: "Let's cap credit card interest rates and save Americans money."

national.title: AP source: FBI investigating apparent hack of its key national criminal justice database
national.summary: The National Crime Information Center, known as the NCIC, is a computerized database of criminal justice information that is available to local, state and federal law enforcement agencies and includes records on fugitives, missing persons, criminal history data, stolen property and other topics.
national.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The FBI is investigating an apparent hack of a national law enforcement database that it maintains, a person familiar with the matter said Saturday.

The National Crime Information Center, known as the NCIC, is a computerized database of criminal justice information that is available to local, state and federal law enforcement agencies and includes records on fugitives, missing persons, criminal history data, stolen property and other topics.

The FBI declined to comment Saturday on the apparent hack, which was first reported by CNN and confirmed to The Associated Press by a person familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak by name and spoke on the condition of anonymity.

Asked about the subject on Saturday, President Donald Trump said in a Fox News Channel interview: "We just heard about it and I will say that it's not good."

WATCH: Mounting tech disruptions raise concerns about U.S. cybersecurity

News that the NCIC was targeted comes as the country has encountered a series of digital outages in the government and private sector that Trump administration officials have said were caused by routine efforts to upgrade computer systems and fix vulnerabilities, rather than a cyberattack. There was no immediate indication that the FBI incident was related to those outages.

The bureau has historically been a frequent target for hackers.

In September, for instance, the FBI said it was investigating a hack of its job portal website after a criminal hacking group known as ShinyHunters claimed it had obtained a massive trove of data on bureau employees and applicants.

national.title: Bayer reaches Roundup settlement that could cost the company billions
national.summary: The money will go to thousands of people who have been or will be diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma – a blood cancer linked to the herbicide.
national.body:
The agrochemical and biotech giant Bayer has agreed to pay billions of dollars to people who sued the company alleging the weed-killer Roundup caused their cancer.

On Friday, a judge in Missouri gave final approval to the nationwide settlement that could cost the company up to $7.25 billion in the coming years.

The money will go to thousands of people who have been or will be diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma — a blood cancer that they claim is linked to glyphosate, which is the main ingredient in Roundup.

Under the settlement in circuit court, people affected could receive anywhere from $10,000 to $165,000 in compensation, depending on whether their work in agriculture or other occupations exposed them to higher levels of glyphosate, the age when they were diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma and other factors.

In a statement , the CEO of Bayer, Bill Anderson, called the settlement a "decisive milestone" that will "mitigate the risks" of pending and future litigation.

The presiding judge, Timothy Boyer, said it was "among the largest in the history of mass tort personal-injury class action settlements."

Law Supreme Court heard case on how to label risks of popular weed killer Earlier this year, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in favor of Bayer, the German company that now owns Monsanto, finding that it could be shielded from lawsuits filed in state courts over claims that it failed to warn consumers about the cancer-causing effects of glyphosate.

The attorney representing the plaintiffs, Christopher Seeger, said in a statement that "Today's final approval order delivers guaranteed compensation to Roundup cancer victims who have waited more than a decade for justice."

national.title: A doctor's guide to surviving — and enjoying — holiday feasting while on GLP‑1 medication
national.summary: Changes in appetite, smaller portion tolerance, limits on alcohol consumption, medication side effects and the desire to maintain progress can make navigating holiday traditions feel a little different.
national.body:
Reed Berger-Fleishman, The Conversation Reed Berger-Fleishman, The Conversation

Thanksgiving and the winter holidays bring celebration, connection and plenty of opportunities to come together with family and friends.

But the holiday season also brings something else: more food-centered gatherings, larger portions and richer foods than most people typically eat throughout the year. Think whipped sweet potatoes, mac and cheese, decadent side dishes and an abundance of desserts.

For people taking GLP-1 medications for diabetes management, weight loss or other medical reasons, these celebrations can present unique challenges. Changes in appetite, smaller portion tolerance, limits on alcohol consumption, medication side effects and the desire to maintain progress can make navigating holiday traditions feel a little different.

WATCH: As GLP-1s reshape America, questions and new uses emerge

As a physician specializing in obesity medicine , I encourage my patients to view GLP-1 medications as an advantage during the holidays. These medications can help regulate appetite, improve awareness of fullness, and reinforce healthier eating behaviors during a season when food often takes center stage.

However, these medications don't eliminate the possibility of overindulgence. In fact, patients who previously experienced little or no nausea due to GLP-1s may suddenly develop significant nausea or even vomiting after eating beyond their new comfort level. Nothing can derail a holiday celebration quite like an upset stomach. Accounting for how these medications affect your body can help you avoid uncomfortable surprises while still enjoying the foods and traditions you love.

Whether taken by injection or orally, GLP-1 medications have become increasingly popular worldwide for managing Type 2 diabetes , obesity and other chronic conditions. In the United States, approximately 1 in 10 adults used these drugs in 2025, and prescribing rates continue to climb.

national.title: Russia-bound ship attacked in Gulf of Finland
national.summary: Finnish defence forces say that Ukraine was likely behind the drone attack on the vessel.
national.body:
A Russian cargo vessel bound for the country's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad has been hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland, Russian and Finnish authorities say.

The ship - the Sparta II - caught on fire after the strike on Saturday morning, before drifting into Finnish waters. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.

"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."

Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones had been used, based on preliminary information, and there was "no threat" to the territory's supplies.

The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.

The company says on its website that it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.

Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.

This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.

national.title: Storms expected on both coasts threatens Thanksgiving travel
national.summary: The mayor of San Francisco is asking people in the city not to travel unless "absolutely essential." Meanwhile, a storm moving up the Eastern seaboard could also cause travel delays ahead of Thanksgiving.
national.body:
Before worrying about the temperature of the turkey, travelers could face a different type of uncertainty next week. This time , it's the weather — and it's affecting both U.S. coasts.

"I know there's a lot of travel for many of you as you head into the Thanksgiving holiday, but I'm going to ask you all to consider not traveling unless it is absolutely essential," said San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie on X Friday . He said the city is preparing this weekend for extreme high tides and rain that could hit the area Monday afternoon through Wednesday.

Over the past week, cities in California saw mudslides, waterspouts and flooding while Florida also saw coastal flooding and inundated streets. A new set of storms are expected to hit both sides of the country early next week, just as travelers head into the holiday week.

It's already been a wet fall in large swaths of the country, thanks in part to a Super El Niño , a natural climate pattern that shifts weather around the world. Devastating flooding in the Southwest U.S. left multiple people dead and hundreds stranded, and California and the Pacific Northwest have seen high sea level and multiple strong atmospheric rivers .

"Take this weekend: get yourself ready," Lurie, the San Francisco mayor, said after a call with the National Weather Service and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

Rain and snow, in higher elevations, is possible over parts of the northwest and northern California on Saturday, according to the NWS .

The West Coast is forecasted to see an atmospheric river, a narrow band of water vapor pushed by the wind, on Monday. Another is expected for the Pacific Northwest later in the week, according to the Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes . Atmospheric rivers hang over an area and dump precipitation. They can cause months worth of rain in just a few days.

The center expects two to four inches of precipitation over northern California and southern Oregon through Wednesday.

ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — Work crews boxed up the venue for this year's United Nations climate talks in Turkey, as negotiators went into overtime on Saturday in an attempt to reach a final agreement on global warming. But hopes are slim that additional discussions will produce concrete plans to slash fossil fuel use.

The added day of talks came as the two-week annual summit, or COP31, drew strong condemnation for failing to mention fossil fuels in a draft of the final agreement. The document is meant to address how the world will deal with climate change, which drives heat waves, floods and other disasters.

To avert the most catastrophic effects of warming, experts said the world needs to urgently and drastically cut emissions from the use of coal, oil and gas.

In a letter sent on Saturday to this year's co-hosts, Turkey and Australia, 100 civil society groups warned that they were "on course to preside over one of the most disappointing COPs" the U.N. has ever held. The letter stated there were only hours left "to save this COP from becoming a low point of three decades of climate negotiations."

A Texas official on Friday defended how the state carried out the execution of a 70-year-old man who loudly insisted he was in pain and pleaded, "Don't let me suffer like this," during a lethal injection that followed a struggle to find a suitable vein.

Yet Reinaldo Dennes' spiritual adviser, who had his hand on Dennes' shoulder inside the death chamber in Huntsville, said he felt like he was holding a bucking bronco Thursday.

national.title: Killer robots: U.N. talks fall short of hopes for legally binding rules
national.summary: U.N. talks in Geneva have failed to deliver binding rules on autonomous weapons, as humanitarian groups warn that military AI is advancing far faster than diplomacy.
national.body:
A Ukrainian FP-1 long-range attack drone is launched at an undisclosed location in Ukraine, Aug. 16, 2026. Efrem Lukatsky/AP hide caption

GENEVA — Diplomats meeting at the United Nations in Geneva have agreed to start discussing options to regulate lethal autonomous weapons, often called "killer robots."

After a week of negotiations that dragged on until the small hours of Saturday morning, a compromise emerged: countries would have two years to suggest regulations that could be legally binding, but could also be optional.

Bleary-eyed negotiators insisted the agreement was better than nothing and showed the U.N.'s disarmament process could still function. But for many humanitarian organizations and many countries, the deal falls far short of what they had hoped for.

Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. That call was backed by the U.N. secretary-general and by Pope Leo .

Their concerns stem from the kind of warfare we are now seeing. In Ukraine, Sudan and Gaza, civilians are being killed by semi-autonomous drones. This year in Sudan , 80% of civilian deaths were caused by drones according to the U.N.

Africa Besieged Sudanese city faces relentless drone strikes and risk of mass atrocities, U.N. warns Humans remain, albeit very remotely, in control for now, but humanitarian organizations fear we are on the verge of seeing artificial intelligence-assisted weapons make the decision to kill entirely on their own.

"There is a fundamental ethical concern with having what are essentially these life-and-death decisions determined by programming, determined by an algorithm," said ICRC legal adviser Georgia Hinds. "That's not something that you can fix with better technology. That is a moral red line that we cannot cross."

national.title: Judge approves $7.25bn settlement for Roundup weedkiller cancer claims
national.summary: The settlement will be paid by Bayer to users who already have non-Hodgkin lymphoma and those who fall ill in the future.
national.body:
A Missouri judge on Friday approved a $7.25bn (£5.5bn) settlement stemming from lawsuits ⁠alleging that Bayer's weedkiller Roundup causes cancer.

Judge Timothy Boyer said the settlement was "fair, reasonable, and adequate".

Bayer, the German bio-tech giant, had proposed paying the $7.25bn to definitively resolve a legal battle in the US.

The nationwide settlement will be paid to Roundup users who are already sick with non-Hodgkin lymphoma and those who fall ill in the future.

The company had already paid roughly $10bn to resolve litigation related to Roundup.

The settlements to participants range from $10,000 to $165,000, depending on how frequently they used the product, when they were diagnosed with the cancer and how severe their illness was.

"[Friday's] final approval order delivers guaranteed compensation to Roundup cancer victims who have waited more than a decade for justice," said Christopher Seeger, a court-appointed counsel for cancer patients in the case.

Bayer will make annual payments into a fund for up to 21 years, providing as much as $7.25bn.

national.title: Federal jury convicts man of starting the deadly 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles
national.summary: Prosecutors argued the defendant, 30-year-old Jonathan Rinderknecht, had been "mad at everything" in the days leading up to the January 2025 fire, which killed 12 people.
national.body:
FILE - Water is dropped by helicopter on the advancing Palisades Fire in the Pacific Palisades neighborhood of Los Angeles, Jan. 7, 2025. Etienne Laurent/AP hide caption

LOS ANGELES — The man accused of sparking last year's deadly Palisades Fire was found guilty of arson charges Friday after his first federal case earlier this year ended in a mistrial.

Jurors convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, of lighting a fire on Jan. 1, 2025, that burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up Jan. 7, becoming one of the most destructive wildfires in California history. The Palisades Fire killed 12 people as it incinerated entire neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Malibu.

Rinderknecht pleaded not guilty to federal charges of destruction of property by means of fire and arson. The scope of the first charge was narrowed to only include the Jan. 1 blaze, known as the Lachman Fire, and the second addresses the Palisades Fire. He was convicted on both charges.

With little apparent reaction, Rinderknecht gave his attorneys hugs before leaving the courtroom. The verdict was delivered on the third day of deliberation.

Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in LA, said the verdict was a "testament of the hard work" his team put into the case. He said he was "intimately familiar" with the strength of the evidence and was happy with the jury that convicted Rinderknecht.

Rinderknecht's attorney Steve Haney said in a statement they were disappointed in the verdict but respected the jury process.

"After a lengthy deliberation, they clearly gave this case a great deal of consideration," Haney said. Regarding an appeal, he said they would review all the options at the right time.

national.title: Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
national.summary: Ukraine's president says Kyiv acted after 109 separate Russian aerial attacks on bridges in Ukraine.
national.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.

In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".

He rejected the claim by the Russian president that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsula it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.

"There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said.

The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.

The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.

This week's combined missile-and-drone strikes by Ukrainian forces destroyed the central road section of the Crimean Bridge, collapsing part of it together with one of the two support arches into the sea and rendering the structure unusable for road traffic.

Russian attacks on Ukraine continued on Friday evening and overnight: a seven-year-old boy was killed in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region. Local officials say he had been in a playground at the time.

local.body:
The Mental Health Association in Chautauqua County (MHA) November recovery luncheon was not only an opportunity to recognize participants for their accomplishments but to express gratitude to staff and volunteers for their service.

As they have for several years, Bonnie Weber, of Be The Change You Want to See in Jamestown, and her volunteers again prepared and served a delicious dinner at the MHA's Thanksgiving luncheon. Working with her were George Brightman, John Case, Shannon Ramirez, and Bill Schmidt. Jon Bogue offered grace.

Among those receiving certificates for their progress were three participants who completed Strong Foundations, an intense 15-week program, using encouragement, practical tools, and community for single parents to build strong, faith-filled homes.

Weber presented roses not only to the participants but to staff as well, in appreciation of their work and commitment. She also recognized volunteers and community supporters, including John Felton, CEO at the Southern Chautauqua Federal Credit Union.

All are encouraged to mark their calendars now for the MHA's second annual fundraiser at the Frewsburg American Legion on Saturday, February 27. Admission will be free, with basket and gift card raffles, a 50/50 drawing, live music, and food and beverages available for purchase.

The Mental Health Association in Chautauqua County is a peer recovery center offering support groups and individual coaching for people looking to improve their lives, deepen wellness, thrive in recovery, or support those on a recovery path. Peers use their personal stories to help people find recovery in their own lives in their own way.

The Jamestown center is at Door 14 in the rear of the Gateway Center, 31 Water Street. Hours are 9:30 a.m.-4:30 p.m. Monday-Thursday and 9 a.m.-4 p.m. Fridays.

The North County recovery center is open Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Thursdays, 9:30 a.m.-4 p.m. in Grace Lutheran Church at 601 Eagle Street in Dunkirk.

local.title: Healing with Horses: Birthday visit can be memorable experience
local.summary: Every parent wants their children to know how special they are. When better to celebrate than on their birthday. local.body:
Every parent wants their children to know how special they are. When better to celebrate than on their birthday.

When my kids started to go to school (in the 1980s), I discovered birthday parties. When it was my daughter's birthday, I did the mom thing and had a party and she invited her friends, and they came. When it was my son's birthday, I tried the same thing, but only one little boy came. It was the boy who was constantly bullied at school. To be his friend meant you were also bullied, but I didn't know any of that then.

Real friendships are built on common bonds and interests, and ultimately, what you get out of a relationship. Who are the friends of children who are different? And when do people really put the feelings of others above themselves?

Today birthday parties can be very creative, and expensive, including taking the party to places outside of the home. It is important to have friends and feel like you belong to a "social" group, but what does it take to make your child feel special these days? And not just that one day, but everyday. I love the "Winnie the Pooh" story of the "unbirthday" celebrations. Then there are 364 days to celebrate with friends instead of just one day. And Eeyore was always included.

But let's go back to the problem of nobody showing up to your party.

Centaur Stride has a program policy to help people make friends and feel special even on their unbirthdays. Friendships and relationships are built on common ground. What does a child with a disability or who is different, neurodivergent or other, have in common with their classmates, cousins or neighborhood kids that is enough to make a bond? One where you have something to talk about, laugh about or just share an experience?

Who doesn't want to go horseback riding? At Centaur Stride, it is definitely not something where social status matters. Our "Friends and Family" program allows a rider to share their lesson with a friend or family member at no additional expense. They can groom a horse together and share ride time. (Instructors must know in advance and all paperwork must be filled out and signed by the participant’s parent.) Would someone say no to a personal invitation like that? During the experience, they can talk about the horse, bond with the horse, and use the horse as a link therapist to bridge a common interest (the horse). Afterwards, in school, at home or in the community, they have a shared experience to talk about on a deeper level than just saying hi. Others who overhear the conversation also usually take an interest and ask questions.

local.title: Little Mice by Dunkirk’s Caleb Spell
Seeking a peace, even for modern-day monsters
local.summary: Like many boys growing up in the 1950s and ‘60s, I was fascinated by monsters. My prized possessions were models of classic horror figures. The stories behind them were thrilling — the battle of the giants King Kong and Godzilla, the rag-clad mummy brought back to life from ancient Egypt, and the ha
local.body:
Like many boys growing up in the 1950s and '60s, I was fascinated by monsters. My prized possessions were models of classic horror figures. The stories behind them were thrilling -- the battle of the giants King Kong and Godzilla, the rag-clad mummy brought back to life from ancient Egypt, and the half-fish, half-man Creature who dwelled in the depths of the Black Lagoon.

Of course I outgrew the toys, but my fascination with malformations of nature never disappeared. There are three classic monster figures which, sixty years later, continue to be a source of dark intrigue for me, mainly because of what they tell us about the nature of man.

As a kid, I favored the Wolfman, in part because I loved dogs. If I was to choose my monster self, it would have been that hairy, agile, dog-like beast who howled at the moon. Later, I began to understand the deeper meaning. The wolfman revealed the violent nature that lurks in our subconscious. As a matter of philosophy, it is a reminder of the need for a social contract (laws) because the threat of violence is always there, just beneath the surface. As a matter of psychology, it echoes Freud's theory of the human psyche (the Id). It is, in short, the Beast Within.

During the '80s and '90s, Bram Stoker's original "Dracula" evolved from sheer grotesque barbarism to assume dark, sado-masochistic qualities. The nature of his evil became refined, sexualized, primed for commercial success. Yet, despite sensationalized Dracula sequels, the themes remain intact. It's essentially about the struggle of good versus evil in the context of Christianity and the Holy Cross.

I was teaching a high school AP literature class when I first took on Mary Shelley's "Frankenstein," perhaps the most challenging novel I've ever read. This is a story that explores the most complex and disturbing aspects of the human condition.

On a dreary November evening, Victor Frankenstein, the obsessed philosopher/scientist, brings to life his creation -- a human-like creature cobbled together with body parts stolen from the graveyard. Victor has created life from the unliving. In so doing, he assumes the role of God. With that role might have come a responsibility, like that of a father to his son -- a sense of duty to protect and provide for. Instead, Victor Frankenstein is overcome with dread and disgust. He abandons his child.

Frankenstein, the monster, enters the world without a name, without family or guidance. In pursuit of his Maker, he acts out, killing Victor's brother and fleeing into the wilderness. Hiding there, he comes upon the simple home of a happy family led by a blind father. During this time, his only period of peace, he spies on the family and learns of the virtues of life and love. Yet his serenity is short-lived, as the family discovers his wretched appearance and drives him back into the woods. His recourse would be revenge, the burning down of the house of love.

Main cast seniors gather backstage after wrapping the closing performance of Clue: High School Edition. From left to right: Eliza Pound (Ms. Scarlet), Bella DeGolier (Mrs. Peacock), JJ Whipple (Professor Plum), Mallory Berndt (Mrs. White), Richard Kuras (Wadsworth).

GOWANDA -- The Gowanda High School Thespian Society successfully wrapped up its production of "Clue: High School Edition" earlier this month, completing a three-show run that delivered a high-energy, campy murder mystery to enthusiastic community audiences.

The production transformed the high school auditorium into Boddy Manor through an innovative moveable set conceived by director Ms. K. Merrill, a student teacher who joined longtime producer Mrs. Nobles to lead the show. Building the iconic rooms -- including the Study, Library, Kitchen, Hall, and Billiards Room -- was a collaborative effort involving the entire cast and crew, led by Garry Smith (Head of Construction and Stage Manager) who brought Boddy Manor from just a concept to the reality of Gowanda's auditorium stage. Beyond the ingenious set design, student actors and crew members executed the fast-paced comedy with sharp, clever timing and detailed staging.

Merrill and Nobles guided the production from concept to curtain call, overseeing set construction, character development, and wardrobe design. Senior actors and leads Mallory Berndt (Mrs. White) and Eliza Pound (Ms. Scarlet) stepped up as Costume Co-Captains, helping their fellow cast members build unique costumes, select props, and develop distinct stage personalities.

Following last fall's production of Knock Knock, the directors sought a title tailored to the talents of their ensemble.

“We have returning students who are instinctively funny, so we wanted something a little more grown-up and witty,” said Merrill.

The final curtain call honored the district’s graduating seniors, marking their final fall play performance on the Gowanda High School stage: Eliza Pound (Ms. Scarlet); Bella DeGolier (Mrs. Peacock); JJ Whipple (Professor Plum); Mallory Berndt (Mrs. White); Richard Kuras (Wadsworth); Amelia Pickering (Sound); Molly Booth (Sound).

local.title: Small pick-up can almost always change a life
local.summary: The call came into the principal’s office a few minutes after 8 a.m. I had completed the daily announcements, done my morning walkabout and checked in with a few needy kids. I was just about to sit down to answer some emails and complete some paperwork when the direct line to my office rang. I […]
local.body:
The call came into the principal's office a few minutes after 8 a.m. I had completed the daily announcements, done my morning walkabout and checked in with a few needy kids.

I was just about to sit down to answer some emails and complete some paperwork when the direct line to my office rang. I recognized the stressed voice on the other end of the line immediately. It was the voice of a woman who had been a student in my math class more than 20 years prior.

She had her troubles growing up and she had given me a run for my money as a student. But I liked her very much. I never took students' misbehavior personally, no matter how insulting, disrespectful or frustrating. And I have never held a kid's missteps against them years later. Who is the same person that they were in middle school? A good educator has to be able to love the unlovable and to have a bottomless well of forgiveness. Anyone lacking in these areas has no business working with kids.

This former student was now struggling as a single mom to raise two spirited daughters of her own. We had communicated numerous times while I worked with this parent as she tried to bring her girls under control. She would tell me that she considered her child rearing struggles as payback for the hell she gave her parents and teachers. And I would chuckle and tell her that she wasn't that bad and neither were her girls.

Mom was having an especially difficult time getting her youngest to come to school. Like many parents, mom had to be at work before her kids got on the bus. And her long work day ended well after school let out.

Her sixth-grade daughter would often pretend to get ready for school, say goodbye to her mother when she left for work and then just stay at home. Other times she would ride the bus to school but instead of entering the building she would walk away and find a place to hang out for the day. Sometimes she would play hooky with a friend at an unsupervised household. On a few occasions daughter was found hanging out at Walmart, McDonald's and other establishments near school grounds. In an effort to get her daughter to school, mom changed her work schedule and started driving her daughter to school.

On this particular morning, my former student was calling from the school drop-off. Her little darling was refusing to get out of the car and come into the building. Mom asked if I could come out to her vehicle and help convince her daughter to come into school. Of course I said yes.

local.summary: Northern Chautauqua Catholic School (NCCS) welcomed hundreds of children, families, and community members last month for an evening of Halloween festivities, family fun, and school spirit at its annual Trunk or Treat and Open House celebration. The event brought together families from throughout the
local.body:
Pictured are participants in the Trunk or Treat and Open House event at Northern Chautauqua Catholic School.

Northern Chautauqua Catholic School (NCCS) welcomed hundreds of children, families, and community members last month for an evening of Halloween festivities, family fun, and school spirit at its annual Trunk or Treat and Open House celebration.

The event brought together families from throughout the community for an evening filled with colorful costumes, decorated vehicles, candy, bounce houses, food, and plenty of smiles. The tremendous turnout reflected the strong sense of community that continues to surround Northern Chautauqua Catholic School.

Earlier in the day, students participated in a schoolwide Halloween Costume Contest, showcasing their creativity and imagination. Students dressed in a wonderful variety of costumes, competing in categories including Funniest Costume, Most Creative Costume, Best Group Costume, and Best Overall Costume.

The evening's Trunk or Treat celebration provided a safe, welcoming environment where children could enjoy Halloween traditions while families connected with friends, neighbors, teachers, and school staff. Visitors also had the opportunity to tour the school and learn more about the educational programs and opportunities available at NCCS.

"We are absolutely delighted by the hundreds of people who came out to celebrate with us," said Ted Sharon, Principal of Northern Chautauqua Catholic School. "Events like this remind us that a school is so much more than a building where children receive an education. It is a gathering place for families, friendships, and community. Seeing so many smiling children and families enjoying themselves was truly wonderful."

The school extends its heartfelt appreciation to the parents, volunteers, faculty, staff, and community supporters who helped make the celebration possible. Special thanks go to everyone who decorated vehicles, donated candy, helped organize activities, and contributed their time and energy to creating a memorable experience for the children.

"To everyone who attended, volunteered, or supported this event in any way, thank you," said Mark Dulak, Head of the Board of Trustees of Northern Chautauqua Catholic School, added. "Your enthusiasm and generosity demonstrate what makes our community so special. We are proud to open our doors to the entire community and look forward to welcoming even more families to NCCS in the future."

local.title: BACK TO THE ROOTS: Gather together, give thanks and celebrate
local.summary: Happy Thanksgiving to one and all! It is almost here, an American holiday that gathers everyone — family or friends to the table to be grateful, to enjoy the fruits of the land, as well as some of our best…
local.body:
Happy Thanksgiving to one and all! It is almost here, an American holiday that gathers everyone — family or friends to the table to be grateful, to enjoy the fruits of the land, as well as some of our best dishes to show off, made by cooks who mostly do not have a culinary degree, for your enjoyment. What better time to celebrate and try new dishes?

One of my granddaughters, Rachel Ruth, in Arizona, shares one of her Thanksgiving dinners she cooked a couple of years back for her family. She is developing into a very fine cook. I am expecting she will be mailing leftovers this year, as she demonstrates her ways with ham a’ la’ Rachel. Rachel’s sous chef is her mother. Ask your grands if they are cooking, or if they would like to learn? It is how we pass on our generation’s wealth, we cook!

Rachel’s breakfast or brunch quiche offering. Easy and healthy to make and delicious on the lips. A great choice for Easter buffets and brunch or anytime you need a really good quiche! This could even be a side main dish for Thanksgiving, if needed.

Butternut squash, sometimes goes by Honeynut, so small and SOOO good. One of my favorites. Tops has them by a bag for $6.

If you know how many folks are coming, that is helpful. If you have to go “ballpark guess,” that is ok too, but make a variety of medium-sized dishes, or if the menu is more limited, cook more in large-volume pans. It is fine to encourage folks to bring a dish to pass if they are able, or a jar of homemade pickles, box of candy, etc. If that ends up not being enough, I usually have a backup dish that is made for later in the week, but can be hauled out, heated and served. Lasagna works well for this. After that, I say, break out the cards, board games and remember that Buffalo is playing on cable. I encourage sharing pictures, both vintage from the past and taking new ones to share at Christmas time. If you have a holiday guestbook, have everyone write their thoughts of the day. Another idea to be used as a hostess, or as a guest at an event, is sharing old garden magazines, catalogs, seeds and giving them out to whoever wants them. Never miss an opportunity to encourage gardening. This idea is transferable to items we no longer use that can be offered to someone else who can. Guests should have the hostess’ permission.

local.title: NIAGARA DISCOVERIES: Benjamin Carpenter, Lockport's first mayor
local.summary: Much has been written about Benjamin Carpenter, the first mayor of the city of Lockport, but every once in awhile we should be reminded of the contributions that were made by many of our forebears who are largely forgotten. Benjamin…
local.body:
A map of Benjamin Carpenter’s quarry property at South Transit Street and State Road in 1851

Much has been written about Benjamin Carpenter, the first mayor of the city of Lockport, but every once in awhile we should be reminded of the contributions that were made by many of our forebears who are largely forgotten. Benjamin Carpenter was born on December 26, 1805 in Orange County, N.Y. His father James died sometime after 1817 and his mother Julia took Benjamin and his three brothers to New Jersey. After four years in that state, they came to Lockport in 1829.

It is not clear what the Carpenter brothers did for a living in Lockport in the 1830s, but Benjamin must have been respected enough to win a seat on the village board in 1834 as a Whig candidate. Six years later, Benjamin and his brother James opened a limestone quarry on the south bank of the Erie Canal just west of Transit Street. Although there were other quarries already in business at the time, the Carpenters’ stone was much sought after for building purposes. Over the next 50 years, the brothers furnished stone for churches, homes, public and commercial buildings, as well as for monuments. It was not only in demand in Lockport and Western New York but across the state and throughout the country.

Ann Marie Linnabery is the assistant director of the History Center of Niagara.

local.title: THE GREAT OUTDOORS: Two great adventures in the swamp
local.summary: With the health issues I have had to deal with over the last three weeks, there have only been a couple of quick photo adventures, but they were great ones.
local.body:
With the health issues I have had to deal with over the last three weeks, there have only been a couple of quick photo adventures, but they were great ones.

I love photographing swans in flight and there is one marsh accessible by vehicle that several trumpeter swan families frequent. Not being able to walk around easily, my photography is done mostly from my vehicle so this spot is ideal. I had been working with the swans in this marsh before I ended up in the hospital but had not gotten exactly the shots I was looking for or messed up on the ones I could have gotten. So, about a week and a half into my recovery, I decided to run over and see if the swans were still using that marsh. Just as I neared the marsh a pair of sandhill cranes were leaving. Darn, just a few seconds late! There was one family of swans on the marsh and I knew there was one other family of six plus another pair of adults that were using that spot so the decision to park and wait for the possible arrival of the others was made. This would offer me some good flight shots as they came in if I did my part. Sitting was still a little painful for me at the time, but what the heck, “No pain no gain.” Maybe the others would show up soon. Well, about an hour into my wait, it happened and a group of six could be heard with their trumpeter calling, heading my way. They didn’t land on their first pass, which was great as it gave me more opportunities to “get it right” on the second circle. Things went well and I was sure good shots were gotten. Of course, the original family got all worked up when the others came in and there was a fight between the two families, which also offered some more unique shots. A short time later, the other pair of adult swans showed up and a few more flight shots were available. My stomach pain was pretty bad by then from twisting around in the seat and sitting that long, so I headed home. Later, the photos were put on the computer and reviewed. I was happy to see what was gotten.

Doug Domedion, outdoorsman and nature photographer, resides in Medina. Contact him at 585-798-4022 or woodduck2020@yahoo.com .

entertainment.title: Britney Spears Apologizes to Her Family on Instagram: ‘I Just Miss Them Like Crazy’
entertainment.summary: The pop star wrote that she regretted raising past grievances publicly, five years after the end of the conservatorship that fractured her relationship with her parents and sister.
entertainment.body:
Britney Spears posted a public apology to her family on Saturday (Nov. 21), writing on Instagram that she regretted revisiting past conflicts in public.

“I’m so very sorry for bringing up past issues, but I think I did because I realized I needed to protect my heart,” Spears wrote. “It’s the way I love, and when I love you, I really love you.” Related Miley Cyrus Marries Maxx Morando in Poolside Ceremony Led by the Flaming Lips' Wayne Coyne Gorillaz Celebrate Mexico's 'Revolutionary Spirit' at Corona Capital, Bring Out Johnny Marr and Trueno BTS, ENHYPEN, BIGBANG & CORTIS Are Big Winners of 2026 MAMA Awards Explore Britney Spears See latest videos, charts and news

She described her own conduct as “childish and embarrassing,” adding: “Thoughts on the past, I’m obviously human, and there actually might be something to those things I said psychology-wise; either way, I’m sorry to my family for bringing up those memories.”

Spears said the conversation had never taken place directly. “I’ve never actually spoken to them face to face on it,” she wrote. “I just miss them like crazy! And I’m very sorry!” She also called herself “blessed to have such a beautiful family.”

Spears is the eldest child of Jamie and Lynne Spears, who are divorced. She has a brother, Bryan, and a sister, Jamie Lynn Spears .

The relationship has been publicly strained for years. Spears spent 13 years under a conservatorship, established in February 2008 with her father as conservator, which gave others control over her finances, career and personal decisions. After an explosive court hearing in June 2021 in which she testified against the arrangement, a Los Angeles judge suspended Jamie Spears that September and terminated the conservatorship on Nov. 12, 2021.

In the years since, Spears has repeatedly addressed the fallout. “Honestly my family embarrassed me and hurt me deeply,” she wrote in December 2021, a month after the termination. Her 2023 memoir The Woman in Me detailed her account of the arrangement, including her view that it “stripped me of my womanhood, made me into a child,” and addressed tensions with her sister.

The sisters’ relationship had already become public: Spears sent Jamie Lynn a cease and desist letter in early 2022 over claims in her sibling’s memoir Things I Should Have Said , published two months after the conservatorship ended. The pair appeared to move toward reconciliation in mid-2023, when Spears posted about visiting the set of Jamie Lynn’s film Zoey 102 .

entertainment.title: Miley Cyrus Marries Maxx Morando in Poolside Ceremony Led by the Flaming Lips’ Wayne Coyne

entertainment.body:
Miley Cyrus married Maxx Morando on Saturday (Nov. 21) in a poolside ceremony in Palm Springs, Calif., with the Flaming Lips ’ Wayne Coyne officiating, one month after the couple sang “Let’s Get Married” together on the Hollywood Bowl stage. Explore Miley Cyrus See latest videos, charts and news

Coyne, who worked with Cyrus on her 2015 album Miley Cyrus & Her Dead Petz and joined her onstage at the Hollywood Bowl in October, led the vows as Cyrus, 33, and Morando, 28, stood beneath an arch of white flowers in front of family and friends, according to photos published by People . Cyrus wore a long-sleeved white satin gown with a high neck, open back and small train, and was photographed wiping away tears during the vows, while Morando wore a black suit. Among the guests were her mother, Tish Cyrus, and husband Dominic Purcell; her sister Noah Cyrus ; and her father, Billy Ray Cyrus , along with Elizabeth Hurley. The celebrations began the night before with a rehearsal dinner, glimpsed in Instagram photos posted by Cyrus’ stepsister Lily-Rose Purcell that showed tables dressed with dark red flowers and small candles, and a menu topped with an “M+M” monogram.

The wedding caps a year in which the relationship moved from the edges of Cyrus’ public life to the center of her work. “Let’s Get Married,” which Morando co-wrote and co-produced, appears on Bass Persuades , her 10th studio album and her first released simply as Miley. Its black-and-white video, directed by Mert Alas and shot at West Hollywood’s Chateau Marmont, casts Morando opposite her — a dress rehearsal, as it turned out, for the real thing two months later.

That album also brought Cyrus back to the top of the Billboard 200, debuting at No. 1 on the chart dated Oct. 3 with 61,000 equivalent album units, according to Luminate. It gave her a sixth No. 1 album and her first since Bangerz in 2013.

It marks a striking shift for a couple who spent years largely out of view. Morando, the drummer for Los Angeles rock band Liily, was first linked to Cyrus in late 2021, when the pair attended a Gucci event together. The two had been set up on a blind date — “Well, it was blind for me and not really for him,” she told British Vogue in 2023 — and he later joined her at the 2024 Grammy Awards, where “Flowers” won record of the year. Morando proposed in October 2025 in a garden on the grounds of their hotel in Kyoto, Japan, telling Wonderland he held out “until the very last moment of the very last day” to keep it a surprise. That iconic juxtaposition of sword-wielding knights and sorcerers in expansive realms saliently evokes the classic archetypes of the genre. Whether its retellings of Arthurian legend or shows riffing on the work of author J.R.R. Tolkien, there is no shortage of medieval fantasy shows. The iconography that comes from these aesthetics are often too rich to pass up and really elevate these types of stories. Many of the shows that we're listing here also happen to be literary adaptations, with best-selling authors using these elements well to widespread fan appreciation. These are the 10 best medieval fantasy shows of all time, exemplifying the appeal of the popular sub-genre.

Trigger/Netflix Let's start off this list with a memorable recent anime series that takes a gastronomic approach to the medieval fantasy genre. Ryoko Kui's manga series "Delicious in Dungeon" was adapted for television in 2024 and is currently available to stream on Netflix. The story follows adventurer Laios Touden who leads an expedition into a sprawling dungeon to rescue his sister from a dragon. Laios also takes the opportunity to try out cooking recipes from fantasy creatures he encounters and slays like mandrakes and animated suits of armor.

If you've ever wondered how to cook certain types of classic fantasy monsters, "Delicious in Dungeon" answers those culinary questions. This odd juxtaposition between medieval action and cooking sequences fuels a lot of the show's self-aware sense of humor. But once the series establishes its strange premise, it brings its more conventionally character-driven fantasy narrative to the forefront. While it may seem silly at first glance, "Delicious in Dungeon" celebrates the genre while providing cooking scenes that are just as entertaining as the combat.

entertainment.title: Tom Selleck Landed Magnum P.I. Thanks To A Western Miniseries With Sam Elliot
entertainment.summary: Magnum, P.I. turned Tom Selleck into a household name, but he never would have gone down in history as a TV legend if he hadn't crossed paths with Sam Elliot.
entertainment.body:
CBS Add TVLine on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Back in the '80s, Tom Selleck rose to fame for his role as Thomas Magnum in "Magnum, P.I." The eight-season crime drama ran for nearly the entire decade, from 1980 to 1988, on CBS. It's old news at this point that the "Magnum" job cost Selleck the part of Indiana Jones in "Raiders of the Lost Ark," but the star never would have nabbed his iconic TV role had it not been for one of the best Western miniseries ever made , which he starred in opposite Sam Elliott: "The Sacketts."

When speaking with Ted Danson at a "Live Talks Los Angeles" event back in August, Selleck recalled the two-part Louis L'Amour adaptation. "I had also done by then a movie — a miniseries called 'The Sacketts,' which was a huge, huge break," the star explained. "So, they knew that I could handle a series." His work on the miniseries provided him with the chance to meet with several writers, including Donald P. Bellisario, ultimately leading to Selleck's vision for "Magnum, P.I."

"It's no exaggeration to say that 'The Sacketts' changed me," Selleck wrote previously in 2024's "You Never Know: A Memoir ― An Actor's Memoir of Hollywood and Television." He went on to add: "That job changed my professional opportunities and my whole outlook on what my appetites might be — and not only as an actor. In all of my life." In fact, the two-part Western led to an on-screen reunion only a few years later.

While the Sackett family was unavailable, L'Amour crafted a new family, the Travens, for his 1982 novel "The Shadow Riders" — and CBS jumped at the chance to get the posse back together. Unlike their previous Western, this horse opera was a made-for-TV feature, adapting only a single L'Amour novel — "The Sacketts" had tackled both "The Daybreakers" and "Sackett." For Selleck, that was more than enough.

"'The Shadow Riders' was not only a sacred trust but a dream come true," he noted. "Maybe that was better than a rest." Selleck shot "The Shadow Riders" between the second and third seasons of "Magnum, P.I.," marking the third and final Western he made with Elliott. The first? Well, Selleck got his first big break on the classic Western series "Lancer," ironically alongside his future co-star.
